series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 1/1] mm/swap: allocate contiguous swap slots for a reclaim batch
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses the issue of scattered swap slot allocations, which can lead to inefficient write requests and increased latency in workloads that rewrite swapped out memory. To mitigate this, it introduces a new approach where contiguous swap slots are allocated for each reclaim batch, following the order-0 allocation strategy. The patch modifies various kernel modules, including mm/shmem.c, mm/swap.h, mm/swapfile.c, and mm/vmscan.c, to implement this new behavior. It also adds new functions to prepare and split swap allocations, as well as updates existing functions to work with the new approach.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch aims to reduce the number of I/O requests on a swap device by keeping reclaim batches contiguous. The current implementation of swap allocation and deallocation can lead to scattered writes, resulting in increased I/O requests. The patch modifies the allocator to allocate contiguous free slots for a reclaim batch, reducing the number of small requests and improving throughput. This is achieved by informing the allocator about the size of the batch and allowing it to allocate contiguous slots accordingly. The goal is to reduce the overhead of swap I/O operations and improve system performance.

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH v2 0/7] btrfs: allocator perf improvements
patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series improves the performance of Btrfs's allocator by reducing unnecessary operations on block groups, particularly in large and mostly full file systems. version_history.subject: [PATCH] mm/page_alloc: let the highest memory node recover from hopeless state

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch fixes a problem where the highest memory node in a system cannot recover from a 'hopeless' state, even when its zone recovers above the high watermark. The issue arises because the current code checks if there is another memory node available for allocations to fall back to by looking at the next higher-numbered node ID, which always returns false for the highest node. This patch changes the check to count the number of nodes with a state of N_MEMORY, effectively checking if any other node exists. As a result, the highest node can now recover from its hopeless state and kswapd will be re-enabled.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 2/6] daxctl: online whole-device memory atomically when available
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the daxctl device control tool to online whole-device memory atomically when available, rather than onlining each block individually. This approach avoids racing issues with other agents that may be online blocks as they appear. The kernel only onlines from an 'unplugged' state, and if this fails (e.g., due to lack of hotremove support), the device is left unchanged and onlined per-block. The patch also updates the per-block path to fail when a device has no memory blocks, rather than reporting zero sections already online.

review_comments.author: Alison Schofield
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer noted that using DAXCTL_KMEM_ONLINE in the atomic --no-movable path could place memory in ZONE_MOVABLE despite --no-movable, and suggested either changing it to DAXCTL_KMEM_ONLINE_KERNEL or adding a zone check

Reviewer noted that a reconfigure-device command may add memory twice, first offline at probe and then daxctl unplugs it and adds it back online, leaving the device unplugged if the re-add fails. Alison suggested transitioning directly from offline to an online state instead of falling back to per-block onlining.
review_comments.raw_body:
Hi Greg, 

A couple of things here...

The atomic --no-movable path uses DAXCTL_KMEM_ONLINE, leaving zone selection
to the kernel. With memory_hotplug.online_policy=auto-movable, IIUC this could
place memory in ZONE_MOVABLE despite --no-movable.

The per-block path checks the resulting zone and fails if it isn't ZONE_NORMAL,
but the atomic path skips that check.

Should this use DAXCTL_KMEM_ONLINE_KERNEL instead, or retain DAXCTL_KMEM_ONLINE
and add the same zone check?

---

With this, a "reconfigure-device -m system-ram" may add the memory twice.
First kmem adds it offline at probe and then daxctl unplugs it and adds it
back online. If that re-add fails, the device is left unplugged rather than
offline.

I get that falling back to per-block onlining would reopen the race this
series is addressing. Could the kernel interface support transitioning
directly from offline to an online state instead? It seems that would avoid
both the extra hotplug work and the left-unplugged failure case.

-- Alison

review_comments.author: Gregory (Meta) (author)

Author acknowledges a technical limitation in their patch due to backward compatibility concerns and expresses willingness to explore alternative solutions, but no clear resolution or fix is planned.
review_comments.raw_body:
This was the intended behavior because otherwise a concurrent
block/state change would end up making the blocks unrecoverable.

---

This is an unfortunate wart for backward compatibility sake.  It would
have been preferable to create the dax device without auto-hotplugging
the kmem region (hotplug but offline), but that would break userspace.

I can take another look whether i can get offline->online to work
internally, but this may still require the hotplug work you're concerned
about.

-- 
~Gregory

series_items.subject: [PATCH 3/6] daxctl: offline whole-device memory via atomic unplug when available
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds the ability to offline whole-device memory via atomic unplug when available, using the daxctl utility. When the kernel provides a 'daxX.Y/state' interface, writing 'unplugged' will atomically offload and remove the device's memory blocks. If all memory is already offline, the operation is still attempted but considered best effort. The patch also updates the 'daxctl list' command to omit 'movable' for devices with no blocks, and removes sysfs directories when unplugging a node's last memory block.

review_comments.author: Alison Schofield
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Alison Schofield noted that the patch changes the behavior of 'daxctl offline-memory' to remove memory blocks entirely, instead of leaving them present but offline, and requested that it keep its existing behavior unless reconfiguring the device.

Reviewer pointed out a potential race condition where another agent could online a block between the check and unplug, suggesting documentation of this edge case for users.
review_comments.raw_body:
Hi Greg,

I see you called this out in the cover letter, and that the kernel is
deliberately combining offlining and removing memory to avoid the race
before unbind.

But, this does change the behavior of the command "daxctl offline-memory".
Previously it left memory blocks present but offline and now it removes
them entirely.

Should offline-memory keep its existing behavior of leaving memory blocks
offline, and use atomic unplug only when reconfiguring the device?

---

When num_on == 0, another agent could online a block between the earlier
check and the unplug and that memory would then be removed.

I see this noted in the commit message. Is that worth documenting for
users?


-- Alison

review_comments.author: Gregory (Meta) (author)
review_comments.summary:
Author pushed back on the reviewer's concern that the patch introduces a race condition by not dropping the per-vswap spinlock before calling try_to_unmap(), arguing that it only matters if daxctl offline-memory changes in this way and that using the atomic interface makes it work.

Author acknowledged a concern about documentation accuracy and agreed to update it.
review_comments.raw_body:
The kernel explicitly does not allow `echo offline > dax/state` because
this just creates the race we're trying to resolve.

I suppose my pushback is: why does it matter that daxctl offline-memory
changes in this way? If daxctl supports the atomic interface, it all just
works. It's a bit more work (additional hot-unplug) but if the memory is
already offline that's not that expensive.

The only scenario I could come up with is having two versions of daxctl
fight with each other (old - no awareness of dax/state, new - uses
dax/state) but is this a real concern?

---

Yes that's intended, and yeah should probably update the docs.

~Gregory

-- 
~Gregory

review_comments.author: Alison Schofield
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Alison Schofield expressed concern that changing the 'offline-memory' behavior would deviate from documented expectations and suggested preserving the existing behavior unless a compelling reason exists to modify it.

Reviewer noted that when all blocks are already offline, the patch should print a message and return success without attempting to unplug, and suggested limiting atomic unplug to the 'daxctl reconfigure-device' path where memory needs to be removed before unbinding dax_kmem.

My concern isn't about 2 version of daxctl fighting. It's about
preserving the documented behavior for "daxctl offline-memory". And just
generally, if there is no need to change it, rather not change it.

---

If all blocks were already offline, print a message and return success
without actually doing anything.

It seems the benefit of atomic unplug is w "daxctl reconfigure-device"
path where memory needs to be removed before unbinding dax_kmem. Could
we limit atomic unplug to that path?

To be clear, I don't know if that (limiting) is doable and I also don't
know if any current user would care either way. I'm just defending the
documentated behavior (FWIW).

review_comments.author: Gregory (Meta) (author)
review_comments.summary: Author addressed a concern about the naming convention for daxctl commands, proposing to rename offline-memory to unplug-memory and reconfigure-device to convert to unplug-memory under the hood. The author acknowledges that this is a result of the default hotplug state being set to 'offline' instead of 'unplugged', but believes it resolves the issue entirely.
review_comments.raw_body:
hm, maybe instead:

daxctl offline-memory      - stays exactly as-is
daxctl unplug-memory       - does the unplug
daxctl reconfigure-device  - converts to unplug-memory under the hood

userland that is suffering from these races can update their scripts

choose between unplugged and some form of online.

I think that resolves the daxctl problem entirely more or less?

-- 
~Gregory

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series introduces support for atomic whole-device hotplug in daxctl using the dax_kmem attribute. This allows for safe and concurrent online and offline operations on a device, preventing races between agents like udev and auto-online. The patch also updates the 'daxctl list' command to report the hotplug state of devices, which can be inconsistent if blocks are toggled individually. The changes maintain compatibility with older daxctl versions and handle cases where unplug or re-adding fails due to lack of memory hotremove support or region reservation issues.

The goal is to enable per-tier resident ratio policies, where the system can prioritize reclaim from specific nodes or tiers based on their temperature (coldness). review_comments.author: Li Zhe
review_comments.summary:
Li Zhe expressed concerns that the patch's approach using source selectors is not a replacement for implementing tiered memcg counters/limits, which would provide accounting and policy targets. He suggested that these directions are compatible and can be used together to improve kernel-driven behavior and user-space reclaim pressure.

Li Zhe noted that the proposed memory.reclaim algorithm does not address the underlying issues of reclaim, such as inverting the LRU and applying per-tier memcg limits, and instead aims to expose a source-scoped proactive reclaim actuator while keeping the kernel's reclaim policy in control. He expressed concern that this approach may be a 'hack' to avoid addressing these harder problems.

Reviewer Li Zhe pointed out that using `source=nodes` in memory.reclaim does not guarantee a one-shot net footprint change and instead requires a feedback loop of applying reclaim pressure, observing the new distribution, and iterating. They also disagreed with constraining zswap pool allocations based on source nodes.

Reviewer Li Zhe expressed concerns that the patch's reclaim interface may be a 'hack' to avoid addressing more fundamental issues in memory management, such as per-tier memcg counters and correct LRU handling. He suggested adding details to the cover letter demonstrating how per-node resident ratios work and requested clarification on what constitutes progress under different scenarios.
review_comments.raw_body:
Thanks for the detailed comments.

I agree that improving the default proactive/async reclaim behavior can
be useful, and I also agree that tiered memcg counters/limits would be
useful. I do not see source=nodes as a replacement for those directions.
They solve different parts of the problem: tiered counters/limits provide
accounting and policy targets, while source=nodes is only an actuator for
proactive reclaim.

So I think these directions are compatible. A better default reclaim
policy or tiered memcg limits can improve kernel-driven behavior, while
source=nodes gives userspace an explicit way to apply reclaim pressure
to a selected resident source.

---

That is fair, and I do not intend this to avoid improving reclaim or
adding better tier-aware memcg accounting. A better memory.reclaim
algorithm would also make source=nodes more useful, because source=nodes
still uses the existing reclaim path after selecting the resident source.
The goal here is narrower: expose a source-scoped proactive reclaim
actuator while keeping the kernel's reclaim policy in control. The old
nodes= discussion had ABI problems, but it also showed that a
nodemask-like source selector is a useful primitive for finer-grained
proactive reclaim control [1].

---

This is a good example of why source=nodes should not be described as a
one-shot net footprint guarantee. Assuming source=nodes:1, the request
applies reclaim pressure to memcg memory resident on node1. That may
free some space on node1 in the short term, which can provide room for a
later node0-to-node1 demotion step. If zswap allocation, kswapd, or memcg
reclaim later moves pressure back across tiers and node1 usage rises
again, that is part of the dynamic reclaim/tiering behavior.

So userspace cannot rely on one write to memory.reclaim to produce a
final per-node distribution. The intended usage is a feedback loop: the
controller observes the memcg's resident distribution, chooses the source
nodes it wants to relieve, applies source-scoped reclaim pressure,
observes the new distribution, and iterates.

I do not think this patch should make source=nodes constrain zswap pool
allocations. That would be a different and much stronger semantic. The
current intent is only to constrain the resident source from which memcg
reclaim applies pressure, while completion accounting remains the
existing memory.reclaim accounting.

---

Agreed. I will update the cover letter to make this model clearer. I
will also make clear that source=nodes is not a final net per-node
footprint guarantee and does not change memory.reclaim completion
accounting.

[1] https://lkml.org/lkml/2022/12/14/194

Thanks,
Zhe

review_comments.raw_body:
On Thu, Oct 22, 2026 at 03:39:29PM -0700, Joanne Koong wrote:
> Every memcg lruvec (per-node) stat update reads the memcg and
> lruvec_stats_percpu pointers in the first 64 bytes of struct
> mem_cgroup_per_node. These updates are extremely frequent (eg these
> updates happen several times for every page that's faulted in, freed,
> dirtied, or written back).
> 
> The memcg_pn_read_mostly cacheline group keeps those read-mostly fields
> on a different cacheline from the lruvec, but Intel CPUs do spatial
> prefetching [1] and fetch cachelines in 128-byte aligned pairs.
> Depending on where struct mem_cgroup_per_node lands in its slab, that
> cacheline can be paired with the cacheline holding the LRU list heads.
> 
> When this happens, every stat update also pulls in a copy of the LRU
> list heads cacheline, which is written to constantly by other CPUs under
> the lru_lock. The stat update has to fetch it from another CPU, which is
> unnecessary overhead since the stat update doesn't use the LRU list
> heads at all. But even worse, the lru_lock holder then has to invalidate
> those copies and wait for the acknowledgements to come back before it
> can do its next write, which makes the lru_lock critical section longer
> for everyone waiting on the lock.
> 
> This was found when analyzing the output of perf c2c for a benchmark
> where many threads fault in pages in one memcg. It showed the first 64
> bytes of mem_cgroup_per_node as the most contended cacheline (over a
> third of all HITMs and 5x more than the lru_lock cacheline) even though
> there are no writes to it. A quick experiment adding extra padding so
> that the cacheline no longer shared a pairing with the LRU list heads
> showed that this removed most of the contention, which confirmed the
> cause.
> 
> Fix this by moving the memcg_pn_cold group, which is only touched when

> Every memcg lruvec (per-node) stat update reads the memcg and
> lruvec_stats_percpu pointers in the first 64 bytes of struct
> mem_cgroup_per_node. These updates are extremely frequent (eg these
> updates happen several times for every page that's faulted in, freed,
> dirtied, or written back).
> 
> The memcg_pn_read_mostly cacheline group keeps those read-mostly fields
> on a different cacheline from the lruvec, but Intel CPUs do spatial
> prefetching [1] and fetch cachelines in 128-byte aligned pairs.
> Depending on where struct mem_cgroup_per_node lands in its slab, that
> cacheline can be paired with the cacheline holding the LRU list heads.
> 
> When this happens, every stat update also pulls in a copy of the LRU
> list heads cacheline, which is written to constantly by other CPUs under
> the lru_lock. The stat update has to fetch it from another CPU, which is
> unnecessary overhead since the stat update doesn't use the LRU list
> heads at all. But even worse, the lru_lock holder then has to invalidate
> those copies and wait for the acknowledgements to come back before it
> can do its next write, which makes the lru_lock critical section longer
> for everyone waiting on the lock.
